subject: business
title: Disruptive Innovation: why well-run companies lose to cheaper, worse products — and when they don’t
dek: Clayton M. Christensen’s theory, from the 1995 Harvard Business Review article with Joseph L. Bower through The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997) to the 2015 HBR restatement “What Is Disruptive Innovation?”: entrants win from low-end or new-market footholds that incumbents rationally ignore, then climb as incumbents overshoot what most customers need. Disk drives, steel mini-mills, Honda’s Super Cub, Sony’s pocket radio, and Netflix versus Blockbuster are the cases; Jill Lepore’s New Yorker critique and the King–Baatartogtokh MIT Sloan study mark the limits.

thumb.alt: Six opened hard disk drives lined up from largest to smallest in front of a ruler.

hero.alt: Six hard disk drives with their cases opened, from an 8-inch drive at the back to a 1-inch drive at the front right, arranged by size along a steel ruler.
hero.caption: Hard disk drives with 8, 5.25, 3.5, 2.5, 1.8 and 1 inch platters, photographed in 2008. Christensen’s theory began in this industry: each step down in size produced drives that were slower and held less than the ones mainstream customers were buying, and in the cases he called disruptive, entrant firms rather than the leaders won the new size. These particular drives illustrate the form factors; they are not the specific models in his data set.

honesty: This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a Christensen biography and not a promise that labeling a rival “disruptive” tells you what to do. The framework is taken from named, public texts: Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen, “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995); The Innovator’s Dilemma (Harvard Business School Press, 1997); and Christensen, Michael E. Raynor, and Rory McDonald, “What Is Disruptive Innovation?” (Harvard Business Review, December 2015), whose wording on footholds, overshoot, the price umbrella, Uber, Netflix, Tesla, and the iPhone is followed closely here. Disk-drive counts (116 new technologies, 111 sustaining, 5 disruptive) and the Seagate and U.S. Steel figures are as reported in Jill Lepore’s June 2014 New Yorker essay “The Disruption Machine,” which quotes the book and then disputes it. Mini-mill margins (about 7 percent gross margin on rebar for integrated mills, 20 percent-plus for early mini-mills, a roughly 20 percent cost advantage) come from the Christensen Institute’s own theory page, not from audited company filings. Honda details come from Richard Pascale’s 1984 California Management Review article and a Harvard thesis on American Honda’s founding; Sony details from the Christensen Institute and the museum label on the photographed TR-55 replica. The Netflix–Blockbuster meeting is Marc Randolph’s own account in his 2019 book That Will Never Work (excerpted in Vanity Fair); Blockbuster’s late-fee share of profits and the 2002 “niche market” quote are as Christensen reported them in How Will You Measure Your Life? (2012), not independently re-checked. The Limits section reports Lepore’s claims and Christensen’s Bloomberg Businessweek reply side by side; it does not settle who is right about every case. The MIT Sloan Management Review finding (7 of 77 cases, 9 percent, matched all four elements) is Andrew A. King and Baljir Baatartogtokh’s, based on expert interviews rather than new financial data. No quotes, numbers, or citations are invented; where a source is paywalled, only what its public pages or authorized copies state is used.

timeline.label: Sony’s first transistor radio
timeline.detail: Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, the company soon renamed Sony, sells the TR-55. Christensen’s later work treats the pocket transistor radio as a new-market foothold: poor sound, but a radio of one’s own for people who had none.

timeline.label: American Honda in Los Angeles
timeline.detail: Honda’s small U.S. team plans to sell larger motorcycles; when those falter, it starts selling the 50cc Super Cub through sporting-goods and other non-motorcycle stores (Pascale, 1984; Harvard thesis).

timeline.label: Mini-mills start at rebar
timeline.detail: Steel mini-mills melt scrap in electric arc furnaces and begin at the bottom of the product range, reinforcing bar, before climbing to structural and sheet steel.

timeline.label: “Catching the Wave”
timeline.detail: Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen introduce “disruptive technologies” in Harvard Business Review, using the disk-drive industry as the main evidence.

timeline.label: The Innovator’s Dilemma; Netflix launches
timeline.detail: Christensen’s book argues that good management causes great firms to fail. The same year Netflix launches a DVD-by-mail service that, by the 2015 account, most Blockbuster customers had no reason to want.

timeline.label: The $50 million offer
timeline.detail: Reed Hastings, Marc Randolph, and CFO Barry McCarthy fly to Dallas and propose that Blockbuster buy Netflix for $50 million. Randolph writes that CEO John Antioco was “struggling not to laugh.”

timeline.label: Netflix “Watch Now”
timeline.detail: Netflix begins streaming films and TV episodes to PCs at no extra charge, rolled out gradually to a subscriber base of more than 6 million (AP report).

timeline.label: Blockbuster files Chapter 11
timeline.detail: Blockbuster files for bankruptcy listing $1.02 billion in assets and $1.46 billion in debt, facing competition from mail, kiosk, and online rivals (New York Times DealBook).

timeline.label: “The Disruption Machine”
timeline.detail: Jill Lepore’s New Yorker essay attacks the theory’s evidence and its spread into schools, hospitals, and newsrooms; Christensen answers in Bloomberg Businessweek.

timeline.label: The test and the restatement
timeline.detail: King and Baatartogtokh’s MIT Sloan Management Review study finds 9 percent of 77 textbook cases fit all four elements; Christensen, Raynor, and McDonald publish “What Is Disruptive Innovation?” and rule that Uber is not disruptive but Netflix was.

timeline.label: Christensen dies
timeline.detail: Christensen dies in Boston at 67 of complications from cancer treatment, CNN reports, citing his brother’s statement to the Deseret News.

read.title: Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen — “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995)
read.note: The first statement of the idea. Opens with Goodyear, Xerox, Bucyrus-Erie, and Sears; builds the argument on disk drives. Paywall possible.

read.title: Clayton M. Christensen, Michael E. Raynor, and Rory McDonald — “What Is Disruptive Innovation?” (Harvard Business Review, December 2015)
read.note: The authors’ own restatement after 20 years: low-end versus new-market footholds, why Uber is not disruptive, how Netflix was, Tesla, the iPhone, and what the theory still cannot explain.

read.title: Jill Lepore — “The Disruption Machine: What the gospel of innovation gets wrong” (The New Yorker, June 23, 2014 issue)
read.note: The best-known critique: handpicked cases, an arbitrary success cutoff, Seagate, Bucyrus, U.S. Steel, the Disruptive Growth Fund, and the spread of the idea to public institutions.

read.title: Drake Bennett — “Clayton Christensen Responds to New Yorker Takedown of ‘Disruptive Innovation’” (Bloomberg Businessweek, June 2014)
read.note: Christensen’s phone-interview reply to Lepore: agreement that the word is abused, fury at her method, and his account of missing the iPhone.

read.title: Andrew A. King and Baljir Baatartogtokh — “How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation?” (MIT Sloan Management Review, Fall 2015)
read.note: Expert interviews on the 77 cases in The Innovator’s Dilemma and The Innovator’s Solution; only seven (9 percent) show all four elements of the theory. Paywall possible.

read.title: Steve Denning — “Fresh Insights From Clayton Christensen On Disruptive Innovation” (Forbes, December 2, 2015)
read.note: Interview published alongside the 2015 HBR article; Christensen explains in plain terms why Uber is a sustaining innovation relative to taxis.

read.title: Christensen Institute — “Disruptive Innovation” (theory page)
read.note: The institute Christensen founded summarizes the Netflix–Blockbuster and steel mini-mill cases, including the rebar margin figures used here.

read.title: Chandrasekar Iyer — “From radios to electric vehicles, targeting ‘nonconsumers’ pays off” (Christensen Institute, November 8, 2018)
read.note: The Sony pocket-radio story as the institute tells it: RCA tried to make transistors match vacuum tubes; Sony sold an inferior radio to teenagers who had none.

read.title: Clayton M. Christensen, James Allworth, and Karen Dillon — excerpt from How Will You Measure Your Life? (HBS Working Knowledge, May 9, 2012)
read.note: “The Trap of Marginal Thinking”: Christensen’s account of Blockbuster’s late fees, its 2002 “niche market” statement, and the basketball story in the fun fact.

read.title: Sean Silverthorne — “Are Crummy Products Your Next Growth Opportunity?” (HBS Working Knowledge, April 21, 2003)
read.note: Christensen previews The Innovator’s Solution: low-end versus new-market disruption, Sony’s transistor radio, and “crummy products for non-consumers.”

read.title: Marc Randolph — “He ‘Was Struggling Not to Laugh’: Inside Netflix’s Crazy, Doomed Meeting With Blockbuster” (Vanity Fair, September 2019)
read.note: Book excerpt from That Will Never Work: the September 2000 Dallas meeting and the $50 million proposal, in the Netflix co-founder’s words.

read.title: Sawdah Bhaimiya — “Netflix’s co-founder says Blockbuster execs tried not to laugh when they pitched a $50 million partnership” (Business Insider, April 19, 2023)
read.note: Business Insider’s report on Randolph’s later retelling; useful for how the story is now told, not as independent evidence of the meeting.

read.title: Richard T. Pascale — “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, Spring 1984)
read.note: Interviews with the Honda executives who opened the U.S. market; the source of the big-bikes-failed, Super-Cubs-sold story. Paywall possible.

read.title: DealBook — “Blockbuster Files for Bankruptcy” (The New York Times, September 23, 2010)
read.note: The Chapter 11 filing: $1.02 billion in assets, $1.46 billion in debt, competition from Redbox, Netflix, and iTunes.

fun_fact.title: The theorist who would not play the final
fun_fact.text: In How Will You Measure Your Life? (2012), Christensen tells how his university basketball team in England reached the final of its big tournament, and the championship game was set for a Sunday. At sixteen he had promised never to play on his Sabbath. The coach and every teammate asked him to break the rule just this once; he refused and sat out. His teammates won anyway. He tells the story in the same passage where he blames Blockbuster’s paralysis on marginal-cost thinking: the cost of “just this once” always looks small, and the full cost arrives later. His conclusion was that it is easier to hold a principle 100 percent of the time than 98 percent of the time.

glossary.explain: Christensen’s term for the process by which a smaller company with fewer resources successfully challenges established incumbents: it starts in a low-end or new-market foothold with a product most incumbent customers consider inferior, then improves until mainstream customers switch.

An improvement that makes good products better in the eyes of an incumbent’s existing customers, from small steps (a fifth razor blade) to breakthroughs. The 2015 HBR article says incumbents usually win these contests.

A starting market made of the least demanding customers, whom incumbents overshoot. An entrant serves them with a “good enough,” cheaper product. Steel mini-mills and discount retailers are Christensen’s examples.

A starting market made of nonconsumers: people who previously went without the product because it was too costly or inconvenient. Personal copiers, the transistor pocket radio, and the PC are Christensen’s examples.
People who cannot or do not buy a product at all because existing offerings are unaffordable, unavailable, or too complex. Serving them is the basis of a new-market foothold.
When incumbents improve products faster than many customers can use the improvement, leaving less demanding customers overserved and open to a simpler, cheaper offer.
Toward more demanding and more profitable customers. Disrupters move upmarket from their foothold; incumbents retreat upmarket rather than fight at the bottom.
The path, not a single moment, by which an entrant’s offering improves from the fringe to the mainstream. The 2015 article insists disruption is a process.
Christensen’s description of a disrupter’s early product: worse on the dimensions mainstream customers value, but adequate for the overserved or unserved customers it targets.

The budgeting and approval routines through which a company decides which projects get money and people. In the disk-drive interviews these routines favored high-margin sustaining projects for known customers and starved small disruptive ones.

The shelter created when high-priced incumbents keep prices up, letting several low-cost entrants profit in a foothold market. When incumbents leave, the umbrella disappears and entrants are pushed upmarket by price competition.
The context of customers, suppliers, and cost structure within which a firm competes. Low-end disrupters start inside an existing value network; new-market disrupters build a new one.
How a company creates, delivers, and earns money from what it sells. The 2015 article stresses that disrupters often win with business models very different from incumbents’, not just new products.

Evaluating a choice only by its extra cost and revenue, ignoring sunk and fixed costs. Christensen argued it pushes incumbents to reuse existing assets instead of building what a disruptive business needs.
Christensen’s paradox: the practices that make a company successful — listening to best customers, investing in the highest-margin opportunities — are the ones that make it miss disruptive threats.
A small steel plant that melts scrap in an electric arc furnace instead of making iron from ore. Christensen’s standard low-end disruption case.
A large steel plant that makes iron from ore and coke in blast furnaces, then converts it to steel. The incumbents in the mini-mill story.
A furnace that melts scrap steel with electric arcs from graphite electrodes; the enabling technology of mini-mills.
Reinforcing bar for concrete: the lowest-margin, least demanding steel product and the mini-mills’ first foothold.
Revenue minus the direct cost of producing what was sold, as a share of revenue. The rebar story turns on integrated mills earning about 7 percent on it.

Pouring molten steel directly into a continuous strand instead of separate ingots. The 2015 article says its slow improvement explains why mini-mills took more than 40 years to match the largest integrated makers.
A device that stores data on spinning magnetic platters. Christensen’s doctoral research tracked the industry as drives shrank from 14 to 8, 5.25, 3.5, 2.5, and 1.8 inches.
A semiconductor device that amplifies or switches electric signals. Early transistors could not match vacuum tubes in power, which suited small pocket radios but not furniture sets.
The glass-tube amplifier used in radios and televisions before transistors; larger, hotter, and more powerful than early transistors.
The U.S. bankruptcy process under which a company reorganizes its debts while continuing to operate. Blockbuster filed in September 2010.

Christensen’s recommended defense: a unit operating under senior-leadership protection, apart from the core business, to pursue a disruptive model. The 2015 article admits: “Sometimes this works—and sometimes it doesn’t.”

In the 2015 article, a business model built on expert judgment, like a general practitioner diagnosing symptoms, contrasted with a “process” model that follows standardized protocols, as convenient-care clinics do.

sections.title: The puzzle: capable leaders keep losing to weaker products

blocks.text: The January–February 1995 Harvard Business Review article that introduced the idea opened with a list, not a theory. “One of the most consistent patterns in business is the failure of leading companies to stay at the top of their industries when technologies or markets change,” Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen wrote in “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave.” Goodyear and Firestone entered the radial-tire market late. Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. Bucyrus-Erie allowed Caterpillar and Deere to take over the excavator market. Sears gave way to Walmart. None of these companies was obviously lazy, careless, or short of money. That was the puzzle the article set out to explain.

Christensen came to the question through a single industry. He entered the doctoral program at Harvard Business School in 1989 and joined its faculty in 1992, Jill Lepore notes in her 2014 New Yorker essay on the theory, and his doctoral research tracked the disk-drive industry, where product generations turned over fast enough to watch leaders rise and fall within a decade. The 1997 book that grew out of that work, The Innovator’s Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail, argued that the leaders did not usually fall because they made bad decisions. They fell because they kept making the good decisions that had made them leaders: they listened to their best customers, invested where margins were highest, and passed over small markets that could not move their revenue.

blocks.caption: Clayton M. Christensen at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Davos, 23 January 2013, during a televised session on decision-making. A portrait of the theory’s author two years before his 2015 HBR restatement of it.

blocks.text: The book reached a wide audience at the right moment. Bloomberg Businessweek later noted that it became a bestseller in 1999, at the height of the dot-com boom, because it seemed to describe the threat e-commerce posed to established companies. By 2015 Christensen, Michael E. Raynor, and Rory McDonald could write that executives at Intel, Southern New Hampshire University, and Salesforce.com treated the theory as a guide. They also complained that “too many people who speak of ‘disruption’ have not read a serious book or article on the subject.” This capsule follows their definitions closely for that reason: the word is now used so loosely that the framework only helps if its terms are kept narrow.

sections.title: Sustaining versus disruptive, two kinds of foothold, and a climb nobody contests

blocks.text: The theory starts by splitting innovation into two kinds. A sustaining innovation makes good products better in the eyes of an incumbent’s existing customers. The 2015 HBR article gives ordinary examples — “the fifth blade in a razor, the clearer TV picture, better mobile phone reception” — and stresses that sustaining innovations can be small steps or major technical breakthroughs. What they share is that they help firms sell more to their most profitable customers. In these contests incumbents usually win, because they have the customers, the money, and every reason to fight. The authors report that in Christensen’s disk-drive study only 6 percent of entrants pursuing a sustaining strategy succeeded. How new or impressive a technology is does not decide which kind it is.

A disruptive innovation is initially considered inferior by most of an incumbent’s customers. The 2015 article defines disruption as “a process whereby a smaller company with fewer resources is able to successfully challenge established incumbent businesses.” Mainstream customers do not switch merely because the new offering is cheaper. They wait until its quality rises enough to satisfy them, then adopt it and happily accept the lower price. The entrant’s early product is worse on the dimension the mainstream values most — capacity, sound quality, selection, speed — and better on something else, usually price, size, simplicity, or convenience.

Disruptions start in one of two places that incumbents overlook. A low-end foothold exists because incumbents keep improving products for their most demanding customers and overshoot what less demanding customers need; an entrant can serve those customers with a cheaper, good enough product. Steel mini-mills and discount retailers are the authors’ examples. A new-market foothold exists where people are not buying at all. The 2015 article’s example is photocopying: Xerox charged large corporations high prices for high performance, while school librarians, bowling-league operators, and other small customers made do with carbon paper or mimeograph machines until personal copiers arrived in the late 1970s. The transistor pocket radio and the personal computer, the authors add, were largely ignored by makers of tabletop radios and minicomputers because they were aimed at nonconsumers of those goods.

Why do well-run incumbents let this happen? The 2015 article lists the reasons in the order researchers found them. First, a company’s strategy is shaped by the customers who provide its revenue, so incumbents sensibly listen to existing customers and concentrate on sustaining innovations. Second, that focus becomes part of the company’s routines. Interviews with disk-drive managers showed that resource allocation processes favored sustaining projects, which had high margins and large markets with well-known customers, while “inadvertently starving” disruptive projects meant for smaller markets with poorly defined customers. No executive had to decide to ignore the threat; the budgeting system did it. Third, the numbers look right at every step. The Christensen Institute’s account of steel puts the integrated mills’ gross margin on rebar at about 7 percent. Handing that business to a mini-mill and shifting capacity to higher-margin products was sound financial management — until the higher-margin products were attacked too.

Christensen later added a reason about how incumbents count costs. In How Will You Measure Your Life? (2012) he described executives who understood a disruptive threat but refused to build, for example, a new sales force to sell the disruptive product, because reusing the existing one looked far cheaper. Standard finance teaches managers to compare marginal costs and ignore sunk ones, and the marginal cost of reusing existing assets almost always looks lower. Entrants have no existing assets, so their only question is what the new business needs. The result, he argued, is that incumbents with more capital find the new venture expensive while entrants with less capital find it straightforward.

blocks.alt: Line diagram with time on the horizontal axis and quality on the vertical axis: two rising solid lines for a previously dominant technology and a new technology, crossing a band between two dashed lines labeled user quality expectations.
blocks.caption: A simplified version of the model in The Innovator’s Dilemma. The dashed band is the range of quality users can make use of; the solid lines show how each technology improves. The established technology climbs above what most users need (overshoot). The new technology starts below the band, serving only undemanding customers, then rises into it — the point at which mainstream customers begin to switch. Drawn by a Wikimedia contributor from Christensen’s model, not reproduced from the book.
blocks.credit: Johan Jönsson (Julle) / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: The diagram captures the theory’s central timing claim: products improve faster than customers’ needs grow. That is how the incumbent overshoots, and it is also how the entrant eventually becomes good enough. The 2015 article explains why entrants keep climbing instead of staying comfortably at the bottom. A foothold market usually holds several similar entrants, not one. While incumbents still sell there at high prices, they provide a price umbrella under which all the entrants can profit. When the incumbents rationally leave, the umbrella disappears and the entrants compete on price. The strongest ones improve their products and move upmarket, where they can again compete against higher-cost incumbents. “The disruptive effect drives every competitor — incumbent and entrant — upmarket,” the authors write.

Four qualifications from the same article keep the framework honest. Disruption is a process, not a product at a moment: the first minicomputers were disruptive because of the path they followed from the fringe to the mainstream, and complete substitution can take decades — more than 50 years after the first discount department store opened, traditional department stores still operate. Disrupters often win with a different business model, not just a different product. Some disruptive paths fail; the theory “says very little about how to win in the foothold market.” And “disrupt or be disrupted” is bad advice: incumbents should keep investing in their core customers while creating a separate division, protected by senior leadership, to pursue the new model.

sections.title: Disk drives, mini-mills, a 50cc Honda, a pocket radio, and a red envelope

people.name: Clayton M. Christensen
people.text: Harvard Business School professor. Built the theory from disk-drive data, published The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997), and restated it with Raynor and McDonald in 2015.

people.name: Joseph L. Bower
people.text: Co-author of “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, 1995), the first statement of the idea.

people.name: Michael E. Raynor and Rory McDonald
people.text: Raynor co-wrote The Innovator’s Solution (2003); both co-wrote the December 2015 HBR restatement that ruled on Uber, Netflix, and Tesla.

people.name: Marc Randolph and Reed Hastings
people.text: Pitched Blockbuster in September 2000. Randolph’s memoir That Will Never Work (2019) is the source of the meeting story.

people.name: Kihachiro Kawashima
people.text: Ran Honda’s first U.S. operation; the Harvard thesis on its founding credits him with pushing the Super Cub through sporting-goods and other unconventional stores.

blocks.text: Disk drives are where the theory was built. As Lepore summarizes the book, Christensen studied the era from the late 1970s when drives shrank from 14 inches to 8, then to 5.25, 3.5, 2.5, and 1.8 inches. He counted 116 new technologies, classed 111 as sustaining and five as disruptive, and found that each of the five introduced “smaller disk drives that were slower and had lower capacity than those used in the mainstream market.” The best-known example is Seagate. In the mid-1980s Seagate delayed making 3.5-inch drives, which makers of portable and laptop computers wanted, because its biggest customer, IBM, wanted a better and faster 5.25-inch drive for full-sized desktops. Seagate did not ship 3.5-inch drives until 1988, which Christensen treats as too late. The case shows the mechanism in its simplest form: the leader did exactly what its most important customer asked.

Steel mini-mills are the standard low-end case. In the Christensen Institute’s account, mini-mills began in the mid-1960s to melt scrap in electric arc furnaces, a process that cut costs by about 20 percent. At first their steel was good enough only for rebar, the reinforcing bar set in concrete, the lowest-quality and lowest-margin product in the market. Integrated mills earned about 7 percent gross margin on rebar and were glad to give it up; the early mini-mills earned 20 percent or more on the same product. The mini-mills improved and moved into higher grades, eventually structural and sheet steel, and each time the integrated mills found it more profitable to shift to higher-margin products than to build mini-mills of their own. By the early 2000s, the institute says, mini-mill companies like Nucor had disrupted integrated steelmakers such as Bethlehem Steel and U.S. Steel. The climb was slow: the 2015 HBR article says continuous-casting technology improved so gradually that it took more than 40 years before Nucor matched the revenue of the largest integrated steelmakers.

The incumbents were not idle. As Lepore quotes the book, U.S. Steel cut its labor from nine hours per ton of steel in 1980 to just under three hours per ton in 1991, and its workforce from more than 93,000 to fewer than 23,000. In Christensen’s telling, even that efficiency drive could not stop the mini-mills, because the integrated mills were improving at the top of the market while the entrants kept taking the product tiers beneath them.

blocks.alt: Panoramic view of a steel mill yard under a blue sky, with long tan industrial sheds, overhead conveyors, stacked steel, and a forklift in the foreground beneath a freeway viaduct.
blocks.caption: Nucor Steel Seattle, photographed in June 2019 from Avalon Way SW. It is a scrap-melting electric-arc-furnace mill whose main product is reinforcing bar — the kind of mill the theory describes. Nucor bought this long-established plant rather than building it, so it is not one of Nucor’s original mini-mills.
blocks.credit: Joe Mabel / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Honda’s entry into the United States shows a new-market foothold that the entrant almost missed itself. In The Innovator’s Dilemma, Christensen lists the small off-road motorcycles that Honda, Kawasaki, and Yamaha brought to North America and Europe as disruptive compared with the powerful road bikes made by Harley-Davidson and BMW. The fullest account of how Honda got there is Richard Pascale’s 1984 California Management Review article, built on interviews with the executives who ran the entry. Honda’s small team in Los Angeles, from 1959, planned to compete with larger motorcycles. When those bikes ran into trouble on American roads, the team turned to the 50cc Super Cub, which it had not planned to push, and found that the stores that wanted it were not motorcycle dealers.

A Harvard thesis on American Honda’s founding adds detail. In spring 1960 the retailer Montgomery Ward offered to sell 650 Super Cubs a year; Kihachiro Kawashima turned the offer down and instead had his sales team place bikes in sporting-goods stores, hardware stores, fishing-goods stores, and lawn-mower repair shops, later backed by the “Nicest People” advertising campaign. Those outlets reached shoppers who were not walking into motorcycle dealerships at all. In the theory’s terms, Harley-Davidson had no reason to respond: its customers did not want a 50cc bike, and its dealers could not make money selling one.

blocks.alt: A restored first-generation Honda Super Cub in blue-grey with a brown seat and pale leg shields, on a museum display platform with a sign asking visitors not to touch.
blocks.caption: A first-generation Honda Super Cub (1958 model) on museum display in Japan. This is the step-through 50cc design that Honda’s Los Angeles team ended up selling through non-motorcycle stores; the photographed bike is a preserved example, not one of the U.S. units.

blocks.text: Sony’s transistor radio is the new-market case Christensen returned to most often. In the Christensen Institute’s telling, early transistors could not handle the power needed for furniture radios and floor-standing televisions, which ran on vacuum tubes. RCA and other leaders worked to make transistors match vacuum-tube quality so they could serve their existing customers, people who could afford high-end electronics. Sony instead built a pocket radio that suited the transistor’s limits and sold it to people, many of them teenagers, who were happy to have a small radio with inferior sound because the alternative was no radio of their own. As transistors improved, Sony moved into larger and better products and competed with the leaders directly. HBS Working Knowledge’s 2003 report on a Christensen talk at a Harvard entrepreneurship conference summed up the lesson as a mock mission statement: “We make crummy products for non-consumers.”

blocks.alt: A small green-and-cream transistor radio with a perforated speaker grille and tuning dial, displayed above a Japanese museum label reading Transistor Radio TR55, 1955.
blocks.caption: A replica of the TR-55 (1955), Sony’s first transistor radio, made under its earlier name Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo; the label names Sony as the owner. It says the transistor radio turned the radio from one fixed set per household into a device people could carry anywhere and listen to on their own — the nonconsumption a new-market foothold starts from.
blocks.credit: ブルーノ・プラス / Wikimedia Commons / CC0

blocks.text: Netflix versus Blockbuster is the case the 2015 article uses to show that disruption takes time. When Netflix launched in 1997, its service did not appeal to most of Blockbuster’s customers, who typically rented new releases on impulse. Netflix had an online-only interface and a large inventory, but mail delivery meant films took several days to arrive. It appealed to only a few groups: “movie buffs who didn’t care about new releases, early adopters of DVD players, and online shoppers.” The authors are explicit that if Netflix had stayed there, Blockbuster’s decision to ignore it “would not have been a strategic blunder.”

Blockbuster had a clear chance to buy its way out. In September 2000, Marc Randolph writes in That Will Never Work, he, Reed Hastings, and CFO Barry McCarthy flew to Blockbuster’s Dallas headquarters to propose that Blockbuster buy Netflix for $50 million and let Netflix run the online side of the business. When Hastings named the price, Randolph saw CEO John Antioco “struggling not to laugh.” The Christensen Institute puts Blockbuster’s revenue in 2000 at more than $5 billion, $800 million of it from late fees. Christensen argued in 2012 that the two companies made money in opposite ways. Blockbuster profited when customers returned films late — analysts estimated, he wrote, that 70 percent of its profits came from late fees — while a Netflix subscriber paid a monthly fee and Netflix did best when discs sat unwatched. By 2002, he wrote, Netflix had $150 million in revenue, and Blockbuster said publicly that online rental was “serving a niche market.”

blocks.alt: A Netflix DVD mailer with a red Netflix logo and a business-reply return envelope addressed to the nearest Netflix shipping facility, next to a disc in its paper sleeve.
blocks.caption: A Netflix DVD mailer and return envelope, photographed in 2006. Mail delivery was the foothold’s weakness — days of waiting, no impulse rentals — and the reason Blockbuster’s new-release customers had little interest at first.

blocks.text: The turn came with a new enabling technology. In January 2007, the Associated Press reported, Netflix began offering streaming films and TV episodes on PCs at no extra charge through a “Watch Now” feature, rolled out gradually to a subscriber base of more than 6 million. The 2015 article says streaming eventually made Netflix appealing to Blockbuster’s core customers, “offering a wider selection of content with an all-you-can-watch, on-demand, low-price, high-quality, highly convenient approach. And it got there via a classically disruptive path.” Had Netflix attacked Blockbuster’s core market from the start, the authors argue, Blockbuster would probably have mounted a vigorous and perhaps successful counterattack. On September 23, 2010, Blockbuster filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, listing $1.02 billion in assets and $1.46 billion in debt.

blocks.alt: Storefront of a Blockbuster video store with large yellow block letters on the roof and window posters reading Best Selection and Newest Releases.
blocks.caption: The Blockbuster store in Bend, Oregon, in August 2018, by then the last remaining Blockbuster Video location. The window still advertises what the 2015 HBR article says Blockbuster’s customers wanted — “Newest releases,” rented on impulse — the need Netflix’s early mail service could not meet.

sections.title: Uber, Tesla, and the iPhone: the authors grade their own theory

blocks.text: The 2015 article spends its opening pages on a company almost everyone called disruptive. Uber, founded in 2009, was operating in hundreds of cities in 60 countries, with a funding round implying an enterprise value near $50 billion. Was it disrupting the taxi business? “According to the theory, the answer is no,” the authors wrote. Uber did not start in a low-end foothold, which would have meant taxis had overshot customers by being “too plentiful, too easy to use, and too clean.” It did not start with nonconsumers either: it launched in San Francisco, a well-served taxi market, among people already in the habit of hiring rides. Its service was rarely described as worse than a taxi, and taxi companies were responding with their own hailing apps and legal challenges, which is how incumbents react to sustaining threats. Christensen put it more bluntly to Steve Denning at Forbes: “Relative to the taxi industry, Uber is a sustaining innovation.”

The authors did not claim Uber would fail. They called it an outlier and pointed to regulation: in many cities entry and prices were so tightly controlled that taxi companies had rarely innovated and could not respond quickly. They also noted that UberSELECT, cheaper than a traditional limousine but without advance reservations, sat at the low end of the black-car market — the one place where Uber looked like a disrupter.

Tesla got the same treatment. Its foothold was at the high end of the car market, among customers willing to spend $70,000 or more, a segment incumbents cared about. If the theory was correct, the authors wrote, Tesla faced either acquisition by a much larger incumbent or “a years-long and hard-fought battle for market significance.” The iPhone was sorted into both categories. At its 2007 launch it was a sustaining innovation in smartphones, aimed at the customers incumbents already wanted and winning on product superiority. Its later growth, they argued, was disruptive — not to other phones but to the laptop as the main way people went online, enabled by a business model that connected app developers with users.

That reading was a correction. In 2007, Lepore reports, Christensen told Businessweek that “the prediction of the theory would be that Apple won’t succeed with the iPhone.” In his 2014 Bloomberg Businessweek interview he explained that he had first seen the iPhone as a sustaining product in the phone market and missed that it was disruptive to laptops. “I just missed that,” he said. “And it really helped me with the theory, because I had to figure out: Who are you disrupting?” The episode shows both the theory’s use and its risk: the same framework can support opposite predictions depending on which market an analyst decides the product is competing in.

sections.title: A good explanation of the past, a weaker guide to the future

blocks.text: The strongest public critique came from a historian. In “The Disruption Machine,” published in The New Yorker’s June 23, 2014 issue, Jill Lepore argued that the theory rests on handpicked case studies and that the cases are weaker than they look. Christensen’s original research, she noted, defined “successful firms” as those that reached more than $50 million in revenue in constant 1987 dollars in any year between 1977 and 1989 — a cutoff he himself called arbitrary. Seagate, the textbook incumbent that missed 3.5-inch drives, doubled its sales to $2.4 billion between 1989 and 1990, and by 1997, the year the book appeared, was the largest company in the disk-drive industry, with revenues of $9 billion. Many of the celebrated entrants were gone: Micropolis failed shortly after its disruptive leap, and MiniScribe collapsed after a 1989 fraud investigation.

blocks.alt: Jill Lepore, with short blond hair and dark-rimmed glasses, speaking to camera in a video still, seated in front of an orange chair.
blocks.caption: Jill Lepore in a May 2020 video recorded for the Library of Congress. The Harvard historian and New Yorker staff writer wrote “The Disruption Machine” (2014), the best-known critique of the theory. A still from a U.S. government video: a portrait of the critic, not a scene from the 2014 debate.
blocks.credit: Library of Congress / Wikimedia Commons / Public domain

blocks.text: Lepore pressed the same objection across other industries. Several of the “new entrants” in the excavator case had been making cable-operated shovels for years, and Bucyrus-Erie, the old-line maker Christensen writes about most, grew its sales sevenfold and its profits twenty-five-fold between 1962 and 1979; in 2011 Caterpillar bought it for nearly $9 billion. In steel, she argued, Christensen left out that U.S. Steel’s workforce was unionized while the mini-mills’ generally was not, and that 22,000 of its workers did not go to work during a 1986–87 labor action — and in 2014 the largest U.S. steel producer was still U.S. Steel. On prediction she was sharper still: the $3.8 million Disruptive Growth Fund that Christensen launched on March 10, 2000, lost 64 percent in less than a year, while the Nasdaq lost 50 percent, and was quietly liquidated. Her broader point was that “disruptive innovation can reliably be seen only after the fact,” and that schools, hospitals, and newspapers have obligations that make them unlike disk-drive makers: “People aren’t disk drives.”

Christensen answered within days, by phone, to Drake Bennett of Bloomberg Businessweek. He began by agreeing with her about the word: in its first pages, he said, the essay seemed to be trying “to rein in this almost random use of the word ‘disruption,’” and he was “delighted that somebody with her standing would join me.” Then he turned on her method, arguing that she had engaged with the 1997 book but not the later work that refined it, and calling the essay “a criminal act of dishonesty — at Harvard, of all places.” Slate’s summary of the exchange observed that the two agreed on one thing: “disruption” had become a cliché.

The most systematic test came the next year. In MIT Sloan Management Review’s Fall 2015 issue, Andrew A. King and Baljir Baatartogtokh took the 77 cases listed in The Innovator’s Dilemma and The Innovator’s Solution and interviewed 79 experts on them. They tested four elements of the theory: that incumbents were improving along a trajectory of sustaining innovation; that they overshot customer needs; that they had the capability to respond; and that they floundered as a result of the disruption. Experts agreed that incumbents floundered in about 62 percent of the cases, but only seven of the 77 cases — 9 percent — showed all four elements. Where experts on a case disagreed, the authors gave the theory the benefit of the doubt.

The 2015 HBR restatement conceded several of these limits in its own words. The theory began as “a statement about correlation” and only later developed a causal explanation. “Universally effective responses to disruptive threats remain elusive,” they wrote, and of their own recommended separate division: “Sometimes this works — and sometimes it doesn’t.” And: “Disruption theory does not, and never will, explain everything about innovation specifically or business success generally.” Read together, the critics and the authors leave a narrower, more useful tool. It explains why a well-run incumbent can rationally ignore a weak entrant, and it tells you which questions to ask before calling anything disruptive. Where did the entrant start? Are incumbents really overshooting? Could they respond if they chose to? Is the entrant on a path upmarket, or only nibbling at the edge?

Earlier Saturday capsules overlap here in specific ways. Jobs to Be Done, Christensen’s later framework, explains what a foothold customer is trying to get done; disruption explains how that foothold grows. Blue Ocean Strategy also looks past current customers to noncustomers, but it redesigns the value curve rather than tracking a trajectory from below. In Playing to Win terms, a disrupter’s foothold is a deliberate where-to-play choice that incumbents decline to contest. And the David and Goliath capsule’s underdog is literal here: Christensen called Netflix “the quintessential David going up against the Goliath of the movie rental industry.”

sections.title: The word spread; the theory narrowed

blocks.text: Christensen spent the rest of his career refining and extending the idea. The Innovator’s Solution (2003), written with Michael E. Raynor, focused on how to build new-growth businesses and developed the distinction between low-end and new-market disruption; previewing it in 2003, he told a Harvard audience that “basically any stock you wish you have owned started out as a disruptive company.” He and co-authors applied the theory to schools in Disrupting Class, to health care in The Innovator’s Prescription, and to universities in The Innovative University — the extensions Lepore attacked most sharply. The 2015 article kept that thread, treating online learning as a possible disruptive path in higher education and describing convenient-care clinics that follow standardized protocols, a “process” business model, as a disruptive alternative to the doctor’s solution shop.

Meanwhile the word escaped the theory. The 2015 article included a Factiva count showing English-language articles using “disruptive innovation” or “disruptive technology” rising steeply in the years before 2015. Its authors wrote that disruption theory was “in danger of becoming a victim of its own success,” used “to describe any situation in which an industry is shaken up and previously successful incumbents stumble.” Their correction was to insist on the narrow definition: a disruption begins in a low-end or new-market foothold, and success is not part of the definition.

Christensen died in Boston on 23 January 2020, at 67, of complications from cancer treatment, CNN reported, citing his brother’s statement to the Deseret News. The framework that outlived him is most useful in the plain form he and his co-authors gave it in 2015: sustaining improvements usually favor incumbents; disruptions start where incumbents are not looking and win by improving along a path the incumbent has sound financial reasons not to follow. Whether a particular company fits is a factual question about its customers, margins, and trajectory — not a compliment.

sections.title: Which competitor are you ignoring for good reasons?

blocks.text: Pick the rival your best customers would never switch to today. What is it worse at, what is it better at, and how many years of improvement would it need before your median customer — not your most demanding one — found it good enough?
